::: {.lead}
*Moon Diver* is a mobile game with eight stages. A small robot, Pip, dives
into a deep lake on the Moon to find lost crystals before the base loses
power. The writer of the studio has the story, but the stages are in the
wrong order: the biggest danger comes too early, and the player gets bored
in the middle. In lecture 3 you learned the building blocks of a story and
the three acts. In this lesson you use them as tools for **analysis**: you
place the story on the stages of a game, list its beats in a table, and draw
its tension as a curve. Then you can see what works, what does not, and how
to put the stages in a better order. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary story-beat narrative-structure three-act-structure inciting-incident climax story-resolution interest-curve hook stakes player-experience >}}

## 4.1 From three acts to the stages of a game

A film tells its story in minutes. A mobile game tells it in **stages**
(levels, chapters or worlds). The player plays one stage, stops, and comes
back the next day. So the writer must decide which part of the story each
stage tells. The order of these parts is the **narrative structure** of the
game.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.1 — Narrative structure"}
The **narrative structure** of a game is the order in which the important
events of its story are placed across its stages or levels.
:::

The three acts give a simple first map (@fig-stages). In a game with eight
stages, about a quarter is act 1, about a half is act 2, and about a quarter
is act 3:

- **Act 1 (stages 1–2):** the normal world, the tutorial and the inciting
  incident;
- **Act 2 (stages 3–6):** the journey, with harder and harder obstacles;
- **Act 3 (stages 7–8):** the climax and the resolution.

![The three acts on the eight stages of Moon Diver.](images/acts-on-stages.png){#fig-stages width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.1 — The acts of Moon Diver"}
1. **Act 1:** in stage 1 the base alarm rings: power at 20 %. Pip learns to
   dive in shallow water (the tutorial). In stage 2 Pip finds an old map: the
   crystals are at the bottom of the Deep Lake (the inciting incident).
2. **Act 2:** stages 3 to 6 take Pip through ice caves, a calm cave garden,
   an attack of ice eels, and dark water where the lamp fails.
3. **Act 3:** in stage 7 a giant guardian protects the last crystal (the
   climax). In stage 8 the base lights come back on (the resolution).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A tutorial with no story. If stage 1 only says "swipe to dive", the player
has no reason to come back. Even a tutorial can start the story: the alarm
and the low power give the player a reason to learn to dive.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The acts of your game"}
Choose a mobile game with stages, levels or chapters that you have played.

1. Write the first four or five stages (or chapters) of the game.
2. Mark the act of each one. Find the stage with the inciting incident.

*Your result:* a list of stages with their acts, and one sentence: which stage
starts the conflict?
:::

## 4.2 The beat table: what happens in each stage

To analyse a structure, the writer lists the story stage by stage. Each
important event is a **beat**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.2 — Story beat"}
A **story beat** is one important event of a story that changes the
situation and moves the story forward.
:::

A **beat table** has one row for each stage (@tbl-beats). It shows the story
beat, what changes, and the new gameplay of that stage. A good beat always
*changes* something: a new place, a new danger, a new skill, a new
piece of information.

| Stage | Story beat | What changes | New gameplay |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Alarm | the base alarm rings: power at 20 % | the stakes are clear | learn to dive |
| 2 The map | Pip finds an old map of the Deep Lake | the goal is clear | read the map |
| 3 Ice caves | Pip finds the first crystal | the journey starts | narrow tunnels |
| 4 Cave garden | Pip repairs its lamp among glowing plants | a calm rest | collect light seeds |
| 5 Eel attack | ice eels chase Pip | a new enemy | escape at speed |
| 6 Dark water | the lamp fails | Pip is alone in the dark | move by sound |
| 7 The guardian | a giant guardian protects the last crystal | the final danger | a boss chase |
| 8 Lights on | Pip returns; the base lights come back | the new situation | none: a short scene |

: The beat table of Moon Diver. {#tbl-beats}

![One row of the beat table as a stage card: the stage, the beat, what changes and the new gameplay.](images/beat-card.png){#fig-beat width=80%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.2 — Finding a weak beat"}
The first draft of *Moon Diver* had this row: *Stage 5 — more enemies*.

1. Is it a story beat? No. "More enemies" is gameplay; nothing changes in
   the story.
2. The writer asks: *what changes for Pip?* Answer: the ice eels wake up
   because Pip took the first crystal.
3. New row: *Stage 5 — ice eels chase Pip (a new enemy, caused by Pip's own
   action) — escape at speed.* Now the gameplay has a reason.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing only gameplay in the "story beat" column: "harder jumps", "more
coins". The player remembers a game by what *happened*, not by how many
enemies there were.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A beat table"}
Use the same game.

1. Make a beat table with four columns: stage, story beat, what changes, new
   gameplay.
2. Fill in four stages. If a stage has no story beat, write "none".

*Your result:* the table, and one sentence: which stage has the weakest beat?
:::

## 4.3 The tension curve: is the game boring in the middle?

The testers of the first draft said: "Stage 3 was the scariest. After that
it got boring." To see why, the writer gives each stage a **tension** value
from 1 (calm) to 10 (very tense) and draws them as a graph. Schell calls such
a graph an **interest curve** (@fig-curve).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.3 — Interest (tension) curve"}
An **interest curve** is a graph of how strong the player's interest or
tension is at each moment or stage of a game.
:::

Good stories and good games often have the same shape:

1. a **hook**: a strong start that catches the player at once;
2. a rise with short **rests**: the tension goes up, but calm moments let the
   player breathe;
3. the **peak** at the climax, near the end;
4. a quick fall in the resolution.

![A good tension curve (Moon Diver, final version) and a weak one (the first draft).](images/tension-curve.png){#fig-curve width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.3 — Two versions of Moon Diver"}
Tension of the eight stages, from 1 to 10:

1. **First draft:** 3, 4, **9**, 5, 5, 5, 6, 2. The peak is in stage 3, and
   stages 4 to 6 are flat. The player meets the guardian too early and gets
   bored later.
2. **Final version:** 6, 5, 4, **2**, 6, 7, **9**, 2. A hook in stage 1, a rest
   in stage 4, a rise to the peak in stage 7, and a short resolution.
3. The writer moved the guardian from stage 3 to stage 7 and added the calm
   cave garden as a rest.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that more tension is always better. A curve that stays at 9 or 10
tires the player, and then even the climax does not feel special. The rests
make the peaks feel high.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/curve-builder.html" poster="sims/curve-builder.png" title="Curve Builder: draw the tension of eight stages" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Curve Builder"}
Open the **Curve Builder** simulator above (or scan its QR code).

1. Load the first draft of *Moon Diver*. Read the feedback.
2. Then set the tension of the stages of your own game (from your beat
   table) and read the feedback again.

*Your result:* your eight values, the feedback of the simulator, and one
change that would improve your game's curve.
:::

## Case study: building the stages of Moon Diver

*Moon Diver* is a made-up mobile game. Pip, a small robot, dives into the
Deep Lake on the Moon to bring back the lost crystals before the base loses
power. The game has eight stages: **Alarm** (the base alarm rings, power at
20 %), **The map** (Pip finds a map of the Deep Lake), **Ice caves** (the
first crystal), **Cave garden** (a calm stage; Pip repairs its lamp), **Eel
attack** (ice eels chase Pip), **Dark water** (the lamp fails), **The
guardian** (a giant guardian protects the last crystal) and **Lights on** (the
base lights come back). The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these stages. In the mini-game below the stage cards are shuffled: you put
them in an order that makes a good narrative structure, and the game draws
the tension curve of your order.

{{< sim file="sims/stage-order.html" poster="sims/stage-order.png" title="Stage Order: build the structure of Moon Diver" kind="game" height="660" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapter on interest curves
and the chapter on story; McKee, *Story*, HarperCollins, 1997, on beats,
scenes and the shape of a story.

## Exercises

1. What is the narrative structure of a game?
2. A game has eight stages. Which stages usually belong to act 1, act 2 and
   act 3?
3. Why should a tutorial stage also start the story?
4. What is a story beat? Give one example from a game you know.
5. "Stage 6 — faster enemies." Why is this a weak story beat? Rewrite it.
6. Name the four parts of a good tension curve.
7. A game has the tension values 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10, 9. What is the
   problem?
8. A game has the tension values 3, 4, 9, 5, 5, 5, 6, 2. Where is the
   problem, and how can the writer fix it?
9. *Moon Diver*: which stage is the inciting incident, which is the rest,
   and which is the climax?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The order in which the important events of its story are placed across its stages or levels.
2. Act 1: stages 1–2; act 2: stages 3–6; act 3: stages 7–8.
3. It gives the player a reason to learn the controls and to come back (for example, the alarm and the low power in Moon Diver).
4. An important event that changes the situation; for example, "the bridge breaks, so the hero must find another way".
5. It only describes gameplay; nothing changes in the story. For example: "Stage 6 — the hero's friend is captured, so the enemies now hunt the hero."
6. A hook at the start, a rise with rests, the peak at the climax near the end, a quick fall in the resolution.
7. The tension is high all the time: there are no rests, and the climax does not feel special.
8. The peak is in stage 3, and stages 4–6 are flat. Move the biggest danger near the end (stage 7) and put a rest between rising stages.
9. Inciting incident: stage 2, The map. Rest: stage 4, Cave garden. Climax: stage 7, The guardian.
:::
